title: Truncating a JavaScript string to "4 characters" can produce an unencodable string
assumption: Slicing a string to the first N characters always produces a valid, re-encodable string.

input.display: "Hi \u{1F600}".slice(0, 4) where \u{1F600} is GRINNING FACE (outside the Basic Multilingual Plane)
input.description: A bio/comment preview truncated to a fixed character count for a card or notification, where the full text happens to end exactly on an emoji.

what_goes_wrong: slice(0, 4) cuts between the two UTF-16 code units of the emoji, leaving a lone surrogate. encodeURIComponent() on the result throws "URI malformed", and converting it to UTF-8 (Buffer.from, TextEncoder) silently replaces it with U+FFFD, the replacement character.
why: JavaScript strings are sequences of 16-bit UTF-16 code units, and .length and .slice() count code units. Any code point above U+FFFF (which includes most emoji) is stored as a surrogate pair, and slicing between the two halves leaves a lone surrogate, which is not well-formed UTF-16. Lone surrogates have no UTF-8 encoding, so encodeURIComponent throws, while TextEncoder and Buffer substitute U+FFFD. Python's str indexes by code point, so a character-count slice never splits a code point; but Python code that truncates encoded UTF-8 by BYTE count (common for a database column limit) has the same failure one level down: decoding raises UnicodeDecodeError, or substitutes U+FFFD with errors="replace".

repros.code:
s = "Hi \U0001F600"
print(len(s), s[:4] == s)
b = s.encode("utf-8")
bcut = b[:5]
try:
    bcut.decode("utf-8")
    print("decoded clean")
except UnicodeDecodeError as e:
    print("UnicodeDecodeError")
print(bcut.decode("utf-8", errors="replace"))

fix: Truncate by grapheme cluster (Intl.Segmenter in JS) or at minimum by code point (Array.from(s) or [...s]), never by raw .length/slice() index, when the text may contain astral characters. In Python, never truncate encoded UTF-8 bytes to a fixed byte budget without first decoding, truncating the string, and re-encoding.

test_cases.note: their_function(text, maxLen) that truncates to maxLen UTF-16 units should not hand back a string that crashes when URL-encoded or re-serialized.
